stem.text: A student investigated the effect of temperature on the rate of photosynthesis at two different light intensities. The rate of photosynthesis was determined by measuring the rate of oxygen production of the plant.
Fig. 7.1 shows the result of the investigation.

stem.caption: Fig. 7.1
stem.alt: Graph of rate of oxygen production in mm3 per hour (y-axis, 0 to 4) against temperature in degrees Celsius (x-axis, 0 to 50) for two light intensities. The high light intensity curve rises from about 1 at 10C to a peak of 4 at 30C, then falls steeply to about 0.6 at 50C. The low light intensity curve stays nearly flat at about 0.4-0.45 across the whole range, with a small rise at 50C.

stem.text: With reference to Fig. 7.1, describe and explain the results of the investigation for the plant in low light intensity.

points.text: rate of oxygen produced / rate of photosynthesis, is low / stays constant
alternatives: small decrease in, rate of oxygen produced / rate of photosynthesis ;

points.text: light intensity was the limiting factor / AW ;
(so) less / little, light energy absorbed / photolysis (of water) / photoactivation (of chlorophyll) / light-dependent reactions / photophosphorylation ; R no light energy absorbed

explanation.text: In low light intensity, the rate of oxygen production stays low and roughly constant (with only a small decrease) across the temperature range, instead of rising and falling like the high-light curve. This is because light intensity, not temperature, is the limiting factor: there is too little light available for photolysis/photoactivation of chlorophyll to proceed faster, so the light-dependent reactions (and so overall photosynthesis) cannot speed up even as temperature rises.

reasoningChain: Describe the trend: rate stays low/roughly flat across the temperature range.
Identify light intensity (not temperature) as the limiting factor here.
Explain: too little light means little light energy absorbed, so the light-dependent stage cannot go any faster regardless of temperature.

inferredMistakes.text: Explaining the flat line in terms of enzyme activity/temperature only, missing that the real limiting factor in low light is the light intensity itself, not an enzyme-controlled (light-independent) step.

stem.text: With reference to Fig. 7.1, describe and explain the results of the investigation for the plant in high light intensity above 30 °C.

points.text: rate of oxygen produced / rate of photosynthesis, decreased ;
two paired data quotes with units
because, enzyme / ATP synthase / NADP reductase / oxygen evolving complex, denatured ; A rubisco
change in active site / fewer ESCs ;

explanation.text: Above 30 °C in high light, the rate of oxygen production falls steadily (e.g. from 4.00 mm3 h-1 at 30 °C to 2.55 at 40 °C to about 0.65 at 50 °C). This decline happens because the high temperature denatures an enzyme involved in photosynthesis (such as ATP synthase, NADP reductase, the oxygen-evolving complex, or rubisco), changing the shape of its active site so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes can form and the reaction it catalyses slows down.

reasoningChain: Describe the trend above 30 °C: rate decreases.
Quote at least two paired temperature/rate data points with units from the graph.
Explain using denaturation: heat changes the enzyme's active site shape, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form and the rate falls.

inferredMistakes.text: Describing the decrease without quoting actual numerical data from the graph (with units), which the MS specifically rewards as a separate point.

stem.text: Describe the process that produces oxygen during non-cyclic photophosphorylation.

points.text: light absorbed by, photosystem II / P680
water splits into protons, electrons and oxygen ; A equation

explanation.text: Light is absorbed by photosystem II (P680), causing photoactivation/photoionisation of chlorophyll: an excited electron leaves the chlorophyll. To replace this lost electron, the oxygen-evolving complex (water-splitting enzyme) splits water, a process called photolysis, producing protons, electrons and oxygen.

reasoningChain: Light is absorbed at photosystem II, exciting an electron out of chlorophyll.
The oxygen-evolving complex splits water (photolysis) to replace that electron.
Water splitting releases protons, electrons and oxygen as products.

inferredMistakes.text: Describing the light-independent (Calvin cycle) reactions instead of the specific water-splitting step in non-cyclic photophosphorylation that actually releases oxygen.
